title: How to read on paper again
excerpt: A short guide to printing the long articles you keep meaning to read, and actually finishing them.
content:
Most of us have a list of articles we saved and never opened again. The tabs pile up, the read-later app fills, and the long pieces we cared about most are the ones we never get to. They are too long to read between notifications, so they wait.

Printing them is an old answer that still works. A printed article has an end you can see. It doesn't ping, it doesn't suggest the next thing, and you can write on it. This sample shows what a Screenbreak print looks like, and the rest of this page is a small guide to reading that way.

Pick one article, not ten

Start with a single piece you would be sorry to miss: a long interview, an essay, an investigation. Print it on its own. A short stack you finish feels better than a thick one you put aside, and the next time you print you will know roughly how many pages you read in a sitting.

Length is easy to judge on paper. Before you start you can feel the thickness of the pages, and halfway through you know how much is left without a scroll bar telling you.1

A printed article has an end you can see.

Keep a pencil nearby

Underline the sentence you want to remember. Put a question mark next to a claim you doubt. Write the name of a friend who should read a paragraph. Notes in the margin are faster than any highlight tool, and they stay with the page.

If you like writing in the margins, choose a design with room for it. The Notes margin design sets the text in one column and keeps a wide margin with a light dot grid for handwriting.2

What happens to the page

A web page carries far more than the article. Menus, ads, cookie banners, share buttons, video players and lists of other stories all compete for the same screen. Screenbreak keeps the article and drops the rest, then sets it in a print design.

Charts drawn by code, maths and diagrams are turned into sharp images at print resolution, so they come out as clearly as the photos. Videos become a still frame with a QR code that opens the video on your phone.

Choose a design that suits the piece

Different articles want different pages. A news story with a strong photo reads well as a two-column page with the photo across the top. A long essay is easier in one calm column. A recipe wants its ingredients in a box you can find with floury fingers. Screenbreak suggests a few designs for each article and tells you why, and you can pick any of them or keep your own favourite as the default.

If ink matters, choose Eco print or Riso zine. Both keep photos light and use far less ink than a full-colour page.

Find a place to read

A chair by a window, a train seat, a kitchen table on a Sunday morning. Leave the phone in another room for half an hour. When you finish, you can recycle the pages, file them, or pass them on to someone else.

That is all there is to it. Press the Screenbreak button on any article and it comes out like this.
